opus-5.5.text:
I think what stands out most is his vision, and his willingness to bet on people early. When I joined MMLab, deep learning in computer vision was still taking shape, and he had already built a lab that brought together a remarkable group of students and young researchers. Many of them went on to lead important labs, start companies, or become professors. That doesn't happen by accident. It comes from someone who knows how to spot talent and then gives it room to grow.

He didn't micromanage. He set a very high bar, always pushing for work that mattered rather than another incremental paper, and then he trusted us to figure out how to get there. As a student, that freedom can feel a little scary at first, because no one hands you a problem. But it forces you to develop your own taste: to ask what's actually worth solving.

The other thing is that he thinks in terms of the bigger picture. Beyond the research itself, he cared about whether the technology could leave the lab and have real impact. You can see that in how MMLab's work later fed into industry. That combination of academic ambition and practical sense left a deep impression on me. It shaped how I think about research even now: pick problems that matter, surround yourself with great people, and give them space.

r001.rationale: The response credits Tang with spotting talent, setting ambitious research goals, and thinking about practical impact, but does not say he could identify the principal contradiction in a chaotic situation.

fable-5.1.text:
The first thing that comes to mind is how much he genuinely believed in students. When I was at MMLab in CUHK, he wasn't someone who micromanaged your research. He gave you a direction, and then he trusted you to go find the path yourself. That kind of trust is rare, and it shapes you. You learn to take ownership of your ideas very early.

The second thing is his sense of taste. He had an almost instinctive feel for which problems were going to matter five or ten years later. Face recognition, deep learning for vision, generative models, he was pushing on these before they became obvious. A lot of people are smart, but having that long-range judgment about where a field is heading is something different.

And then there's the human side. He cared deeply about the people around him, about building a community rather than just a lab. Many of the people now leading AI research and companies in China came out of that environment, and I don't think that's an accident. He created a culture where ambition and generosity could coexist. Even today, when I make decisions about my own group, I often find myself asking what he would have done.

r001.rationale: The response describes Tang’s trust in students, research judgment, and community building, but does not say he could identify the principal contradiction in a chaotic situation.

astra-6.text: What stands out to me about Professor Tang is the importance he placed on asking meaningful questions. In research, it’s easy to focus on improving a result, but the deeper question is whether you’re working on something that matters. That’s the quality I most admire in a research mentor: helping people develop their own judgment.
